title: Attention and Transformers: How the Model Reads Context

series.title: What Happens When You Press Enter?
series.subtitle: How ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini Really Work
series.runningPrompt: Write a short poem about the rain

shorts.cta: Full episode: What Happens When You Press Enter? · Stop 5

cues.text: Next stop: Attention Junction! Passport out. Stamped.
This is stop number 5 of seven. In Vector Valley, every word got its own place on a map of meaning. Today, the words start talking to each other.
Here's a puzzle. The word bank can mean the side of a river, or a place that keeps your money.
On its own, the word can't tell you which. The words around it decide.

props.text: “Bank” has two meanings. The words around it decide which one you get.

cues.text: On the route map, we've left Vector Valley, and we're here, at Attention Junction, where the model reads the whole sentence together.
At the end of our last stop, we asked: in "the bank of the river", how does the model know which bank you mean? Let's watch.
In "I sat on the bank of the river", the word bank looks around the sentence, and looks hardest at river. So this is the riverside.
Now: "I paid cash into the bank". This time, bank looks at cash and paid. So this is the money kind.
Same word, same starting vector, but a different meaning, because of what it paid attention to. The percentages on screen are just for illustration, but the idea is real.

sentences.note: Now it looks at “cash” and “paid”: the money kind

cues.text: This trick is called attention. Each word looks at every other word in the prompt, decides how much each one matters to it, and blends in a little of their meaning.
So bank, plus a lot of river, becomes riverbank.
Think of a busy railway junction. Announcements fill the air, but every traveller only listens for the ones that matter to their own train.

props.definition: Each word looks at every other word in the prompt, decides how much each one matters to it, and blends in their meaning.
props.analogy: At a busy junction, every traveller listens only for the announcements that matter to them.

cues.text: Let's try it on our running prompt: "Write a short poem about the rain". What does the word poem pay attention to?
What kind of poem? A short one. About what? The rain. And write tells it this is a task, not a question.
After attention, poem is no longer just any poem. It now carries the idea of a short poem, about rain, that you want written.

sentences.note: What kind of poem? Short. About what? Rain.

cues.text: Pause and predict. "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." What does it refer to? The animal, the street, or the crossing?
The answer is the animal. Streets don't get tired. Animals do.

props.question: “The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired.” What is “it”?
props.explain: Streets don't get tired. Animals do.

cues.text: Watch the word it. With tired at the end, it looks mostly at animal.
Now change just one word: "because it was too wide". Suddenly, it looks at street instead. Animals aren't wide. Streets are.
One word at the end of the sentence changed how a word in the middle was understood. That's attention working across the whole sentence at once.

segments.title: How the model finds “it”
segments.shortTitle: How AI works out what “it” means

cues.text: So how does a word decide where to look? Here's the idea in four small steps, with no formulas.
First, ask. Every word makes a query: a little description of what it's looking for. The word it is looking for a thing that can be tired.
Second, match. Every word also has a key, like a label saying what it offers. The query is compared with every key.
Third, weigh. The match scores are turned into percentages that add up to one hundred.
Fourth, blend. Each word carries a value, its useful meaning, and the asking word mixes in those values using the percentages. Query, key, value: that's the heart of attention.

props.title: Four small steps, for every word

steps.label: Ask
steps.detail: query: what am I looking for?

steps.label: Match
steps.detail: key: compare with every word's label

cues.text: And the model doesn't do this just once. It has many attention heads, each looking at the same sentence in its own way.
One head may follow grammar: who did what to whom.
Another may link a word like it to the thing it refers to.
Another may simply watch the neighbouring words. Nobody assigns these jobs. They're learned during training, and many heads are hard to explain at all.

props.title: Many heads look at the same sentence at once

items.text: One head may follow grammar: who did what
Another may link “it” to the thing it refers to
Another may just watch the neighbouring words

cues.text: Put all of this together and you get a transformer: the design inside almost every modern chatbot. It's a stack of layers, and each layer does two things.
The vectors come in, fresh from Vector Valley.
First, attention: the words look at each other and share meaning.
Then a feed-forward step, where each word thinks on its own for a moment, using what it just gathered.
And then it repeats, layer after layer, dozens of times. With every layer, the understanding of the sentence gets a little deeper.

props.title: A transformer is a stack of layers

steps.label: Feed-forward
steps.detail: each word thinks on its own

cues.text: There is one limit. The model can only pay attention to what it can see. That's called the context window: the most tokens it can look at in one go, including your prompt, the chat so far, and its own answer.
Early chatbots could hold a few thousand tokens. Many today can hold hundreds of thousands.
Think of a desk. Only what fits on the desk can be read at once. Anything that falls off the edge is simply not there.

props.definition: The most tokens the model can look at in one go: your prompt, the chat so far, and its own answer.
props.example: Early chatbots: a few thousand tokens. Today: often hundreds of thousands.
props.analogy: A desk: only what fits on the desk can be read at once.

cues.text: But even inside the window, attention isn't perfectly even. Researchers in 2023 hid a fact at different places in a long prompt, and asked models to find it.
Facts near the start, and near the end, were found most often. Facts in the middle were missed more.
They called it "lost in the middle". Newer models are much better at this, but the habit is worth knowing about.

props.title: Facts in the middle of long prompts get missed more
props.note: Illustrative, after a 2023 study; newer models do better

cues.text: Time for "Try it yourself": a pause-and-guess quiz you can run on any chatbot.
First, ask it: "I saw her duck. What does that mean?" Before it answers, make your own guess. Is it a bird, or someone bending down?
Then add a little context: "I saw her duck behind the wall." Ask again, and watch how a few extra words change the meaning it picks.

steps.text: Ask a chatbot: “I saw her duck. What does that mean?”
Now add context: “I saw her duck behind the wall.” Ask again.

props.chat: I saw her duck. What does that mean?

cues.text: Myth versus reality.
The myth: the model reads your prompt one word at a time, left to right, like we do.
The reality: it reads the whole prompt at once, in parallel. Every word looks at every other word at the same time. Only the answer is written one token at a time, and that's our next stop.

segments.title: Myth vs reality: does it read word by word?
segments.shortTitle: Does AI read your prompt word by word?

props.myth: It reads your prompt one word at a time, left to right
props.reality: It reads the whole prompt at once, in parallel. Only the answer is written one token at a time.

cues.text: And here's your "Use it tomorrow" tip: put key instructions at the start or end of long prompts.
If you paste in a long document, put your main instruction first. For very long prompts, repeat it at the end. And keep the long reference text in the middle.

props.tip: Put key instructions at the start or end of long prompts
bullets: Repeat it at the end of very long prompts
Keep long reference text in the middle

cues.text: Let's stamp the passport. Attention lets every word look at every other word, and decide which ones matter.
That's how bank finds river, and how it finds the animal. Stack attention into dozens of layers and you get a transformer, reading everything inside its context window at once.
So now the model understands your prompt. But how does it pick each word of the answer, and why does it sometimes make things up? Next stop: Prediction Station.
